title: What can this source tell us?
node: AC9HH7S03 n3
summary: "The four questions (origin, content, context, purpose) are used together to decide what a source can and cannot tell us about a particular question. A source is rarely useful or useless on its own: it depends on what you are asking. A stone inscription made to win support is poor evidence of what ordinary people thought of the emperor, but good evidence of how he wanted to be seen."
language: maths
hook: "The First Emperor's inscription says everyone now lives in peace. Can we use it to find out whether people really did? Or can it tell us something else?"
---
You now have four questions to ask of any source.

**Origin**: who made it, when and where. **Content**: what it shows or says. **Context**: what was going on. **Purpose**: why it was made.

On their own they just describe the source. Together, they help you decide **what it can tell you**, and what it can't. That depends on what you want to find out.

## Predict: what can it tell us?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing first shows whether students treat a source as simply true or untrue instead of asking what it can tell us about this question."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "The First Emperor had an inscription cut into stone saying everyone lived in peace under his rule. Can it tell us whether everyone really did?"
  options: ["Not reliably: it praises him, so it mostly shows how he wanted to be seen", "Yes: it was carved in stone for everyone to read, so it must be true", "No: a source that praises a ruler can tell us nothing at all", "Yes: it was made at the time, so it shows what really happened"]
  actual: "Not reliably. Historians think it was made to win support, so it is better evidence of how he wanted to be seen than of what everyone thought. That is still useful."
```

## Try: match the questions to Source C

```step
stage: run
insight: "Matching each of the four questions to its answer for one source shows what each question adds, before the answers are joined into a conclusion."
check:
  type: match
  q: "Match each question to its answer for Source C, the First Emperor's stone inscription."
  pairs:
    - ["Origin: who, when, where?", "Set up by order of the First Emperor, around 219 BCE, on a mountain"]
    - ["Content: what does it say?", "He brought peace, and one set of laws, weights and measures"]
    - ["Context: what was going on?", "The Qin had just defeated six rival kingdoms"]
    - ["Purpose: why was it made?", "Probably to show his power and win people's support"]
  explain: "Each question gives a different piece. You can ask them in any order that suits the source. What matters is that you have all four before you say what the source can tell you."
```

You can ask the four questions in whatever order suits the source. The conclusion comes once you have all four answers, because it is built from them.

## Worked example: Source C

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Using all four answers about one source on one question shows how the conclusion is built, and how to say what a source cannot tell us."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You want to know: What did the First Emperor want people to think of him? Which conclusion about Source C is best?"
      options: ["It shows he wanted to be seen as a ruler who brought peace and order, since it was probably made to win support", "It shows that people across the empire really were living in peace and order", "It tells us nothing about him, because a source that praises him is biased", "It shows how he wanted to be seen, but only because it is a secondary source"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It was made to praise him, so it cannot show what everyone's life was like.", "A source that praises him is very good evidence of how he wanted to be seen.", "It was made during his reign, so it is primary for the Qin."]
      explain: "A source made to win support is good evidence of how its maker wanted to be seen."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Now you want to know: Did ordinary people in the conquered kingdoms like the new empire? What can Source C tell you about that?"
      options: ["Not much: it was probably made to win their support, so it won't show people who disagreed", "A lot: it says everyone lives in peace, and it was made at the time", "Not much, because it is over two thousand years old", "A lot, because the emperor would have known what his people felt"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It says that, but it was made to say that. Ask who made it, and why.", "Age does not decide it. Its purpose does.", "A ruler might not know, and would not carve it if people disliked him. Ask why it was made."]
      explain: "The same source is good for one question and weak for another. Its purpose helps you see which."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which of these is the best way to finish a sentence about what a source can tell us?"
      options: ["'Source C shows how the emperor wanted to be seen, but it cannot show what people really thought.'", "'Source C is true, because it was made at the time the emperor ruled.'", "'Source C is false, because it praises the emperor and leaves things out.'", "'Source C is primary, because it was made on the emperor's orders.'"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Made at the time does not make it true. And true or false does not say what it is good for.", "Leaving things out does not make it false. It limits what it can tell us.", "That says what kind of source it is, not what it can tell us."]
      explain: "A good conclusion names what the source can tell us and what it cannot."
```

## Vary: the same questions on a new source

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Changing the source and the question shows that the same four questions give different conclusions."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You want to know: What rules did Qin officials have to follow? Which source is best, B (laws on bamboo slips) or C (the inscription)?"
      options: ["Source B: it was written for officials, to tell them the rules", "Source C: it was set up for everyone to read", "Source C: it says there was one set of laws", "Neither: both were made by the Qin state, so both are biased"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Being read by everyone does not make it list the rules. Think about its purpose.", "It mentions laws, but only to praise him. The slips list the rules.", "Made by the state does not make a source useless. Rules written by officials are just what this question needs."]
      explain: "Source B was made to tell officials the rules, so it fits the question. Source C was made to show power."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Source D, the 2019 museum label, says the warriors were found by farmers in 1974. Which question is Source D good evidence for?"
      options: ["How the warriors were found in the 1970s", "Why the First Emperor wanted a clay army", "How the craftsmen felt about their work", "What the warriors were made of"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It was written in 2019 by people who were not there. It can only repeat what historians think.", "It was written in 2019 by museum staff, who did not meet the craftsmen.", "For that, the warriors themselves are better evidence than a label about them."]
      explain: "The label is a secondary source about the warriors. It is good for how they were found and how museums explain them today, not for what the emperor thought."
```

## Practise: say what a source can tell us

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Using all four questions on a fresh case, and writing the conclusion in a form that names its limit."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A clay warrior was made for the First Emperor's tomb. Which is the best conclusion about what it can tell us?"
      options: ["It shows what Qin armour and weapons looked like, and how much effort went into the emperor's tomb", "It shows what Qin people believed about life after death, all across the empire", "It shows how Qin soldiers fought in battle and how they won their wars", "It shows exactly what each soldier looked like, because each face is different"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It was made for one man's tomb. It cannot tell us what everyone believed.", "Figures standing in a pit show equipment, not how battles were fought.", "Different faces do not prove each is a portrait of a real person. Historians still debate that."]
      explain: "Its content shows armour and weapons. Its purpose and context show how much effort went into the emperor's tomb."
  - check:
      type: reflect
      text: "I took one source, asked who made it, what it shows, what was going on and why it was made, and then said one thing it can tell us and one thing it cannot."
```

## Make: your own source

```step
stage: make
insight: "Using all four questions in your own words on a source from your own unit is the whole skill."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In my own book I picked a source (from our unit, or one of Sources A to D) and a question, wrote its origin, content, context and purpose, then one sentence on what it can tell us and what it cannot. A partner read it and gave feedback on whether it names a limit." }
```

Write it in your own book or document, not on this page. Your partner or teacher reads it.

## Typical: a source that looks back

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "A secondary source gets the same four questions, but its origin and purpose are modern."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Apply the four questions to Source D, the museum label. Which is the best sentence about what it can tell us?"
  options: ["It shows how museum staff in 2019 explain the warriors, not what Qin people thought", "It tells us what Qin people thought, because museum staff are experts", "It cannot tell us anything, because it was written in 2019", "It tells us the truth about the warriors, because it is in a museum"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Experts can explain the warriors, but they were not there. It cannot tell us Qin people's thoughts.", "Modern is not useless. It is useful for different questions.", "Being in a museum does not make a source true. Labels can be out of date."]
  explain: "The label's origin and purpose are modern, so it can tell us about modern knowledge, not about the Qin directly."
```

## Wider: two sources that look different

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "Different purposes can make different sources give different pictures of the same time."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Source C says everyone lives in peace under one set of laws. Source B lists punishments for people who break the rules. Why might they give different pictures?"
  options: ["They had different purposes: one probably to win support, one to tell officials the rules", "One of them must be wrong, because they cannot both be true", "Source C is from later, after the empire had become peaceful", "Source B was written by enemies of the emperor, so it shows the bad side"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Neither has to be wrong. They were made for different jobs.", "Both were made during the Qin, only a couple of years apart.", "Source B was written by Qin officials. It shows punishments because it was written to tell officials the rules."]
  explain: "Sources made for different jobs show different sides. Together they give a fuller picture than either alone."
```

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
learning: use origin, content, context and purpose together to say what a source
  can and cannot tell us about a question
summary: "Students use all four questions (origin, content, context, purpose)
  together to decide what a source can and cannot tell us about a particular
  question. A source is rarely useful or useless on its own: it depends on the
  question. This gives students a way to say what a source is good for, and
  prepares the next course, which looks at accuracy and usefulness."
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 8 min · Practise 6
  min · Make 6 min. Typical and wider steps are extras and not counted in this.
goals:
  - I can use origin, content, context and purpose on one source.
  - I can say what a source can tell us about a question, and what it cannot.
  - I can write a sentence that names the limit of a source.
struggle: Students say a source is simply true or false, or that it is useless
  because it was made to persuade. Ask 'Useful for what question?' and let them
  argue before you settle it.
before: >
  This lesson puts the four questions together. It has a hinge-friendly check in
  the exit ticket, but the two earlier lessons are the hinges. If students are
  unsure of origin versus content or context versus purpose, go back to those
  lessons before this one.


  The next course in the pathway, Source usefulness, takes up accuracy (fact and
  opinion, reliability) and usefulness (value for a specific question). This
  lesson names the idea, 'what it can and cannot tell us', but does not ask
  students to judge accuracy. Keep them to describing.


  The worked example is ancient China in the Qin and Han period. It is a model:
  swap in your own depth study's sources, keeping the questions the same.
  Everything else is plain-words descriptions, and the museum label (Source D)
  is made up. The purposes of the ancient sources are historians' inferences (no
  Qin text states why the army or the inscription was made), so the lesson says
  "probably". The Try step is a match, not an ordering task: the four questions
  can be asked in any order, and only the conclusion has to come after them.
running:
  - "Predict: ask for votes. The 'carved in stone so it must be true' option is
    a common first thought."
  - "Try: the match has no fixed order. Ask what each answer adds, and why the
    conclusion needs all four."
  - "Worked example: the same source answers two questions differently. Ask
    students what changed between them."
  - "Vary: ask students to name the question first, then the source."
  - "Make: read one or two out if students are happy to, without names."
stuck:
  - see: A student says the inscription is true because it was made at the time.
    ask: Made at the time by whom, and why?
    fix: Go back to its purpose. Historians think it was made to win support.
      Primary does not mean it tells the whole truth.
  - see: A student says a source is useless because it praises someone.
    ask: Useless for what question?
    fix: It is good evidence of how the maker wanted to be seen. Useful depends on
      the question.
  - see: A student's sentence only says 'it is true' or 'it is old'.
    ask: What can it tell us, and what can't it?
    fix: "Use the sentence frame: 'It shows ..., but it cannot show ...'."
stretch: Two sources, one inscription praising the emperor and one list of
  punishments for breaking the law, give different pictures of the same time.
  Why? This is the same idea at greater width. It does not go on to the next
  course.
support: "A card with the four questions and a last line: 'So it can tell us
  ..., but it cannot tell us ...'. Students fill it in for one source."
leads: >
  Next in the How we know pathway: Source usefulness (AC9HH7S04): fact and
  opinion, accuracy and usefulness.


  Also in the pathway: How we know (AC9HH7K08), on digs, dating, written sources
  and conservation.
exit:
  q: "Choose a source from this course and a question. Use the four questions,
    then finish: 'It can tell us ..., but it cannot tell us ...'"
  a: "For example, Source C and the question 'How did the emperor want to be
    seen?': it can tell us he wanted to be seen as a ruler who brought peace and
    order, but it cannot tell us what ordinary people really thought."
explain: >
  Use all four questions together: origin, content, context and purpose. Then
  say what the source can tell you about your question, and what it cannot.


  A source is useful or not for a particular question.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: The inscription says everyone lives in peace. Does that mean they did? What
      would you want to see before you decided?
    prompts:
      - Who made it, and why?
      - What other kind of source might show something different?
    notes: "There is no single right answer. Judge the reasoning: does it use the
      maker's purpose to say what the source can and cannot show?"
  activities:
    - at: investigate
      kind: discussion
      title: Same source, two questions
      minutes: 6
      do: >
        Give half the class the question 'How did the emperor want to be seen?'
        and half 'What did ordinary people think of him?' Everyone uses Source
        C. Compare what each half can say.
      notes: The same source is good for one question and weak for the other. Ask why.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: It can tell us, but it cannot
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Ask each pair to finish one sentence about a source from your unit: 'It
        can tell us ..., but it cannot tell us ...'. Read a few out.
      notes: Listen for a limit that comes from the source's purpose or origin, not
        just 'it is old'.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Which is the limit?
      type: question
      q: Historians think the stone inscription was made to win support for the
        emperor. What is its limit as evidence?
      options:
        - It is unlikely to show people who disagreed with him
        - It is too old to tell us anything useful
        - It is not primary, so it cannot be trusted
        - It is only useful if every word on it is true
      answer: 0
      explain: Its likely purpose is to win support, so it shows how he wanted to be
        seen. It will not show those who disagreed.
```
